newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Swedish groups in controversial merger plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swedish groups in controversial merger plan.

text.p: Swedish insurer Skandia and mortgage bank Stadshypotek on Monday proposed a merger that would create the Nordic region's biggest financial institution but the plan was immediately slammed as unethical by Finance Minister Erik Asbrink.

The announcement from the two firms, in the wake of a government statement that the state would sell its 34 percent Stadshypotek stake through an auction, sparked an unprecedently violent reaction from the usually reserved Asbrink.
"I have no confidence in the present Board of Directors of Stadshypotek," Asbrink thundered in a statement.

Asbrink, angry that Stadshypotek had been negotiating with Skandia without consulttimg him as the largest shareholder, said the country's biggest mortgage lender had strayed into areas reserved for shareholders.
"The Stadshypotek board's behaviour is contrary to what is customary practice in Swedish industry," he said.
"I am very critical to how the board of directors of Stadshypotek has handled this question," he said.'

The share market, sensing a bidding war for Stadshypotek, immediately marked the company's share price up seven crowns to 205 crowns when trading started more than four hours late at 1345 GMT. Skandia eased 2.5 crowns.
Asbrink said expressions of interest in the state's stake in the mortgage lender had been noted from Sweden and abroad.
"We think this one is not over. This is not a done deal yet, considering the way it has been left open by the government." BZW analyst Angus Runciman said.
"Our feeling is that the government has clearly left the way open for a higher bid for Stadshypotek," he added.
Both companies said the Swedish government had not been willing to discuss the proposed merger.

The two companies said in their statement that the new group, to be called Skandia Stadshypotek, would have total assets of about 500 billion crowns ($75.8 billion), net assets of 37.5 billion and a total market capitalisation of about 45 billion as at November 22.
Stadshypotek said 11 of its shares would buy 10 shares in the new company.
The two companies said the merger was expected to improve earnings per share in 1997, generate large cost savings and enhance returns through an expansion of international unit linked business.
On the cost side, savings are expected primarily from the integration of SkandiaBanken and Stadshypotek Bank and merging branches and administration.

The total synergies are estimated at 800 million crowns in 1998 and 1.2 billion in 1999, of which more than half comprises cost savings. Restructuring costs of 500 million crowns over the next three years were forecast.
"We are convinced that the new company will increase value for money for shareholders in Skandia and Stadshypotek," Skandia's chief executive Bjorn Wolrath said.

"We are creating a strong and competitive Nordic financial services company which has the capital base required to meet the challenges of restructuring within the Nordic finance sector demands," Wolrath said.
Skandia chairman Sven Soderberg said Skandia's offer was made in the firm belief that the state would carefully consider the proposal.
He said the government said the restrictions on the sale process as laid down by parliament were the reason the two companies had not been allowed to discuss the proposal with the major shareholder.
Soderberg said in a statement the merger would allow for rapid expansion of AFS (Assurance and Financial Services), Skandia's international life and financial services unit.
He said a 5.0 billion crown cash injection would be needed for AFS over the next five years.
"A merger as proposed creates a strong group with its core markets of savings, mortgages and insurance. The merger also creates good opportunities for a more rapid expansion of AFS."
($1=6.597 Swedish Crown)
